source: Waltz, Lau, Grewal, Holyoak (2000) The role of working memory in analogical mapping
finding: A 7-digit memory load cut relational (structure-based) mappings in cross-mapped picture scenes. Experiment 1, phonological load.
numbers: N=45 undergraduates, 2x2 between-subjects. Relational responses lower with load (M=.35 vs .64; F(1,41)=12.48, p<.01). 3-map prompt .60 vs 1-map .39 (F(1,41)=6.64, p<.05). No load x map-count interaction.
limits: Small cells; digits recalled fully only about 50% of the time. Picture stimuli from Markman and Gentner (1993).
agent_relevance: Under load, models and people fall back to surface-feature matches. Keep relational structure in view, not in a long list to recall.

source: Waltz, Lau, Grewal, Holyoak (2000) The role of working memory in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 2: random-digit generation (executive load) hurt relational mapping, but not more than the simple phonological load.
numbers: 2x3 between-subjects, error df 103. No distraction .45 vs distractor tasks .24 (F(1,103)=23.70, p<.01). Phonological .23 vs random digits .25 (F<1). Main effect of distractor F(2,103)=11.87.
limits: Executive load added no cost beyond the phonological load. Authors infer the phonological buffer is involved in relational processing.
agent_relevance: Load of any kind shifts mapping toward attribute matching.

source: Waltz, Lau, Grewal, Holyoak (2000) The role of working memory in analogical mapping
finding: When relational mapping failed under load, answers were usually attribute-based, not random.
numbers: Only 7.5% of all mappings in Exp 1 were neither relational nor attributional.
limits: Cross-mapped items force a choice between the two kinds of match.
agent_relevance: Error type is diagnostic: a surface-match answer signals overload, not ignorance.

source: Richey, Phillips, Schunn, Schneider (2014) Is the link from working memory to analogy causal?
finding: Ten sessions of complex working-memory training raised trained and near-transfer memory scores but did not change verbal analogy accuracy.
numbers: N=25 trained, 29 controls. Spatial CWM 3.08 to 6.44 (d=3.16); verbal CWM 4.92 to 8.80 (d=1.93). Digit span 8.11 to 8.61 (d=0.69, n=18); spatial WM .81 to .86 (d=0.62). Verbal analogy .55 to .54 (t(24)=.15, p=.88, d=0.10).
limits: Small sample. Transfer distance may be too large. Even high-gain subgroup showed no change (.57 to .57, d<0.01), so a weak-manipulation reading is unlikely.
agent_relevance: Raising raw capacity may not raise mapping quality. Gains likely come from how a scaffold uses capacity, not from more capacity.

source: Richey, Phillips, Schunn, Schneider (2014) Is the link from working memory to analogy causal?
finding: No visual analogy advantage for the trained group versus untrained controls.
numbers: CWM M=.77 (SD .22) vs control M=.76 (SD .17); F(1,50)=0.04, p=.84, d=0.05. Solution times also equal.
limits: Visual analogy given only at posttest, so between-group comparison only.
agent_relevance: Same null as for verbal analogy; supports a threshold view of WM in analogy.

source: Richey, Phillips, Schunn, Schneider (2014) Is the link from working memory to analogy causal?
finding: Background correlational evidence linking working memory to analogy, and the mixed training-transfer literature.
numbers: Kyllonen and Christal (1990), N=399: verbal analogy strongly correlated with three of four WM tasks; digit span r about .30 to .40. Raven's training transfer: some studies find gains, others fail.
limits: Secondhand summary of earlier studies; not independently opened.
agent_relevance: Correlation does not show causation; training WM did not shift analogy.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat college students on text matrix, letter-string, verbal analogy and story analogy tasks, zero-shot.
numbers: Humans: UCLA undergraduates (N=57 on letter-string and verbal analogy; N=80 SPM data from earlier work). Digit Matrices modelled on Raven's SPM. Four task domains.
limits: Authors admit letter-string problems may be on web pages. GPT-3 text-davinci-003. Single-answer accuracy.
agent_relevance: Strong relational mapping in text does not need human-sized WM, but test items may be familiar.

source: Hodel, West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed robustness check: GPT-3 fell sharply when the alphabet was shuffled and letter interval widened, while humans held up.
numbers: Only 2 of 6 problem types (remove redundant, sort) matched original accuracy. Counterfactual comprehension checks: GPT-3 at least 30% of original level except predecessor on synthetic alphabet.
limits: They also argue 'zero-shot' cannot be shown without a training-data audit; ChatGPT could produce letter-string examples.
agent_relevance: Test items must be unfamiliar. Evaluate our scaffold on counterfactual variants, not only standard ones.

source: Lewis, Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Replication with 136 Prolific adults and three GPT models on counterfactual letter-string analogies: humans clearly better.
numbers: Overall accuracy over all alphabets and problem types: humans .753 [.734,.773]; GPT-3 .488; GPT-3.5 .350; GPT-4 .452. 1,876 human samples; 6,840 per model.
limits: Humans scored higher than Webb's humans on original problems. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 no better than GPT-3 (3.5 worse). Temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Chat tuning did not help, even hurt. Do not assume a newer model maps better under unfamiliar symbols.

source: Lewis, Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Error patterns differ: humans mostly use an alternative valid rule or apply a rule in the wrong place; models err differently.
numbers: About 160 manually coded wrong answers per GPT model (5 per problem type and alphabet). Four error classes including alternate rule formation.
limits: Manual coding by authors on a sample; letter-string has no single correct answer.
agent_relevance: Error taxonomy can guide a checker: alternate-rule answers deserve a second look before rejection.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Rebuttal: GPT-4 with code execution solved shuffled-alphabet analogies at roughly human level; failure traced to counting letter positions.
numbers: Humans N=99. Without code GPT-4 worse, on par with HW and LM. Interval-size effect: not significant with code (P=0.066), significant without (P<2e-16); humans P=1.5e-11.
limits: GPT-4 used code only to turn letters into indices. Not a human-like route. 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% in human data.
agent_relevance: Offload index and counting work to a tool; this frees the model for relation mapping. Supports a tool step in the scaffold.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Result was comparable on original and new synthetic alphabets and across two engines with different training cutoffs.
numbers: Logistic regression showed no significant alphabet or engine effect (supplementary figures 2 and 3).
limits: Per-cell N not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Argues against pure memorisation of the original items.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: ChatGPT shows a working-memory limit like humans: d' falls to about 1 at 3-back in verbal n-back.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, temperature 1, 50 blocks per n for n=1,2,3. Capacity about 3 in three variants; noise variant lower.
limits: Spatial capacity lower than verbal. Chain of thought raised scores. GPT-4 higher but not tested above n=3.
agent_relevance: Context length is not capacity: the model has a small effective hold-and-update limit. Keep active items few.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: Instruction strategy and abstract reasoning change capacity but the decline with n persists.
numbers: Abstract-reasoning variant gave significantly lower capacity than base. Open models (Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B, Vicuna-7B/13B) had very low, near-identical capacity.
limits: n-back is a proxy. Main results from one model family.
agent_relevance: Reasoning while holding items costs capacity, as in people. Split mapping into small steps.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: Distractors reduce capacity: noise symbols lowered d' versus the other three verbal variants.
numbers: Noise variant significantly lower; other three variants gave capacity about 3 (d' near 1 at n=3).
limits: Human parallel cited (Gaspar 2016).
agent_relevance: Strip irrelevant tokens before mapping.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits in language models
finding: Across 7 OpenAI models, n-back performance stayed below human level as size grew, so scale alone does not remove working-memory limits.
numbers: Models from text-ada-001 to GPT-4. Larger models gained from advanced prompts (CoT, AutoCoT, SC-CoT, PS, ToT); smaller models did better with answer-only prompts.
limits: Authors note n-back correlates weakly with complex WM tasks (Jaeggi 2010), so it is a rough measure.
agent_relevance: Match prompt complexity to model: heavy scaffolds can hurt weak models.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits in language models
finding: Code-style prompts and rehearsal cues helped some tasks.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard category ii, GPT-3.5: mean over five advanced prompts 67.6% vs 44.4% answer-only. Code prompts boosted text-davinci-002 on structured logic.
limits: Cues such as 'so before that' were hand-tuned per task.
agent_relevance: Recap and rehearsal steps cut dropped items in long lists, a cheap guard.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits in language models
finding: Smaller models lose accuracy with advanced multi-step prompts compared with answer-only.
numbers: Small models (e.g. text-curie) decreased with advanced prompts vs answer-only.
limits: Reported in figure-based discussion.
agent_relevance: Do not apply a heavy mapping routine to a small model blindly.

source: Raemaekers, Finn, De Houwer et al. (2025) Assessing the relational abilities of LLMs and large reasoning models
finding: Preregistered battery (N=1364 problems) of relational syllogisms on nonwords: models good on simple relations, weaker on analogy.
numbers: Same/different: Llama 3.3 70B 70.59%, Llama 3.1 405B 83.16%, GPT OSS 20B 99.32%, GPT OSS 120B 99.80%. Analogy block: Llama near chance, GPT OSS about 83%.
limits: Only four models. No human baseline; normative data lacking. Analogy phrased unusually ('A to B same as B to C').
agent_relevance: Reasoning models handle relation chains well; analogy still a weak spot.

source: Raemaekers, Finn, De Houwer et al. (2025) Assessing the relational abilities of LLMs and large reasoning models
finding: Replication with randomised premise order gave comparable results; 1 to 5 premises barely hurt comparative and temporal relations.
numbers: Near-maximum accuracy on comparative and temporal blocks at all premise counts, for all models.
limits: Block-level descriptive statistics.
agent_relevance: Premise count in this range is not the bottleneck for current reasoning models, unlike human WM limits.

source: Chuderski (2022) Fluid intelligence emerges from representing relations
finding: Rival to the relational-complexity limit: fluid reasoning differences come from valid, robust role-filler bindings, not from how many relations fit at once.
numbers: Argues integration and relational complexity are not the main driver; even simple bindings limit ability. Cites Chuderski (2019) on single trivial bindings.
limits: Theoretical proposal; direct observation of relation encoding is lacking.
agent_relevance: Check binding fidelity (who did what to whom), not only item counts.

source: Chuderski (2022) Fluid intelligence emerges from representing relations
finding: Reference list cites Halford, Wilson, Phillips (1998) relational complexity and Chuderski et al. (2012) storage capacity explains fluid intelligence.
numbers: Citation only; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: Follow up the 1998 BBS paper if capacity numbers are needed.

source: Richland, Morrison (2010) Is analogical reasoning just another measure of executive functioning?
finding: Commentary: analogy depends on executive function but is not merely an executive measure; relational knowledge and inhibition interact.
numbers: Cites Richland et al. (2010) cross-cultural study showing a dissociation between inhibiting featural distractors and integrating relations.
limits: Short commentary, no new numbers.
agent_relevance: Inhibiting surface distractors is a separate skill from holding relations; add an explicit distractor-suppression step.

source: Doumas, Morrison, Richland (2018) Individual differences in relational learning and analogical reasoning: a computational model of longitudinal change
finding: DORA/LISA simulation: varying lateral inhibition reproduced three child learning paths (analogical throughout, non-analogical, transitional).
numbers: Longitudinal geometric analogy data from children over 6 months. Inhibition in both learning and reasoning matters.
limits: Computational account with fitted parameters. I read the abstract and framing, not full tables.
agent_relevance: Frame the limit as interference control, not only slot count.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Authors say GPT-3 shows emergent analogy ability yet may use a fundamentally different mechanism from humans.
numbers: Text states machine intelligence may be fundamentally different from the human kind.
limits: Position statement.
agent_relevance: Treat human WM theory as an analogy, not a spec.
